> List-Archive: <http://www.stat.math.ethz.ch/pipermail/r-sig-s/>
> Date: Mon, 30 Apr 2001 21:41:48 -0400
> 
> John
> 
> >I sympathize, but on the other hand we should try to do as much as
> >possible to make _most_ cases work easily for the programmer.
> 
> Having spent a great deal of time tracking down cases that don't work,
> I'm not so sure that this is a good idea. I like to use functions that
> are defined with a consistent behaviour in mind and are intended to work
> the same way all of the time, not just most of the time.  I realize that
> this is not exactly what you meant to say, but R and S are already
> fairly compatible at a superficial level so I do not think the audience
> for a package like SLanguage will be casual users, and programmers will
> not want to use it if it breaks things that usually work.

We seem to be operating on different wavelengths, but I think that
will be fine, and we can end up with software for both.

It's all very well to assume that the users are just like me, so I can
write what I need to use.  In fact, that's a valid way of proceeding.
For the future, though, this does have to be supplemented if we want
to draw along a larger part of the overall S language audience.  This
is a large group and not all of them can afford the time to learn a
different regimen of programming, at least not until a new generation
of books and manuals is written :-)

I believe we need two approaches, at least for some of the "hot spots"
in compatibility, such as the approach to the search list:

- software that works as the books describe for most cases, in either
  implementation (especially if it can optionally warn about cases
  that are ambiguous);

- alternate software that is part of an unofficial "standard" S
  language and has as consistent a definition as possible.

Notice that complete compatibility is impossible so long as the
semantic models differ in certain basic aspects, so compromise will
always be with us.

> For most users
> it is already easy to write compatible code. (It is mainly a question of
> knowing a few things to avoid.)

Hmm, is it?  It would be interesting to hear opinions from other
subscribers to this list.  I suspect "most users" don't use both systems.  


> >Yes, for sure there are aspects that CAN'T be handled without the
> >programmer worrying explicitly about compatibility.
> 
> I think there may be two levels of compatibility to worry about. As you
> point out, things get rather more complicated if one tries to program
> using environments and language objects. Looking at SLanguage I see that
> most of the things you are working on are things that have not been an
> issue for me, mainly because I have avoided them. Perhaps there is a
> natural way to split this into different pieces.
> 
> What I am thinking about is a much more simplistic level, where
> compatibility should not be an issue but it is. At this level many of
> the problems have to do with the operating system interface rather than
> R/S language differences. Most of these problems are handled just by
> using the R function names and defining functions for S (e.g. Platform,
> Sys.info, Sys.sleep, getwd). In part it is easier to use the R
> definitions in S because backwards compatibility has not been an issue
> in R, and these functions have consistent cross platform definitions. In
> part it is simpler because the names have not been used in S so S/R
> differences are less of an issue. One case (perhaps the only one) where
> this does not work is for unlink.
> 
> >(I just had to revise the get function today to match R usage more
> >accurately)
> 
> Yes, the version I downloaded this morning causes problems in my code.

Something a little more specific would be helpful!  How about
submitting a bug report to http://www.omegahat.org/bugs

BTW, the current version is SLanguage_R_0.1-3.tar.gz, available from
the omegahat R package area,
http://www.omegahat.org/download/R/packages/
--it's usually mirrored on CRAN, but I haven't checked this morning
yet.  Do try the current version.

> Also, the DESCRIPTION file had some errors (it looked like the package
> name and version were suppose to be automatically filled in, but
> weren't) and when you get test code it needs to be in SLanguage/tests
> not SLanguage/inst/tests or "R CMD check" will not run it.

That doesn't sound up to date.  At any rate, I picked up the version
mentioned above today, and R CMD check only warned about a missing
Maintainer field and undocumented objects.

question of
PG> knowing a few things to avoid.)

JC>Hmm, is it?  It would be interesting to hear opinions from other
JC>subscribers to this list.  I suspect "most users" don't use both
systems.

John

It would be interesting to hear opinions from other subscribers to this
list, but I should qualify what I meant a little bit. I meant "most
users" in the sense of numbers of users not users that use the languages
the most. In my sense I expect most users are beginners, fairly casual
users and students. I don't think anyone on this list is in that
catagory. Thus I expect most users do not use both systems, but write
compatible code by accident rather than by design. This is mainly
because they do not use the languages at the level of the concerns you
are addressing in SLanguage. If their code does not run in both S and R
it is more likely because they have used some proprietary Splus
function.

Paul

There appear to be large numbers of students and others who use one system
at `work' and another at `home'.  At their level, I suspect it is
fairly easy to write compatible code, but not as easy as it could be.

My take is that writing compatible code is easier than writing code that
runs efficiently (in some sense) on multiple systems (and I am not
sure that S3 vs R is the main issue here, rather than S3 vs S4).
Often my grad students try two or three systems to see which one
performs the best.

Brian
